Pour que tout le monde sache
You express purpose: pour / afin de + infinitive, pour que / afin que + subjunctive, de peur que / de crainte que + subjunctive, de sorte que.
in order to, so as to
so that, in such a way that
I wrote this speech so that everyone knows who he was.
I’ll speak slowly so as not to cry.
She took notes for fear of forgetting.
Speak loudly, so that the residents can hear you.
We put out chairs so that everyone can see.
To use "pour / afin de + infinitive" when the subject is the same.
To use "pour que / afin que + subjunctive" when the subject changes.
To express a negative purpose (what you want to avoid): de peur que / de crainte que (ne) + subjunctive, de peur de + infinitive.
To tell apart "de sorte que" + subjunctive (purpose) from "de sorte que" + indicative (result).
To talk about a ceremony: inauguration, speech, tribute.
Friday, 15 September, nine in the morning. In a few hours the Salle Henri Bernard will be inaugurated. Odile has written a speech and reads it to Ioana in the kitchen, to rehearse.
Ioana, have you got five minutes? I’ve written a few words for this afternoon. I’d like to read them to you, so that you can tell me if it’s too long.
Of course. Sit down. I’ll make you some tea, so that your voice is nice and warm.
Thank you. So… "Henri wasn’t a great musician. He was a sailor. But he whistled a waltz every 3 May, without ever telling us why."
It’s very beautiful. But why do you start by saying he wasn’t a musician?
So that nobody imagines a great composer. I want people to know who he really was: a simple man who kept a secret all his life.
And Hélène? Are you going to talk about her?
Yes, but I changed one sentence for fear that she’d be embarrassed in front of the journalists. She doesn’t like people talking about her feelings in public.
"This room bears his name so that his waltz never stops. May children play here, sing here, hit wrong notes here. He would have loved wrong notes."
(wipes her eyes) Odile, it’s perfect. Don’t change a thing.
I’m afraid I’ll cry. I’ve written the text in big letters, so that I can read it even if my eyes are wet.
If you cry, everyone will cry with you. I’ve put tissues on every chair, so that nobody is caught unprepared.
(laughs) You really do think of everything. You know, Henri would have adored you.
And I would have adored him too. Come on, finish your tea. We need to leave early, for fear of getting stuck in traffic.
("afin que / afin de" = so that / in order to)
fear ("de peur que" = for fear that)
When the person doing the action and the person with the purpose are the SAME, you use the preposition + INFINITIVE:
I wrote in big letters so that I can read it. (I write, I read)
We need to leave early so as not to get stuck.
Negation with the infinitive: "ne pas" goes BEFORE the infinitive: "pour NE PAS pleurer", "afin de NE PAS oublier".
2. Pour que / afin que + subjunctive (different subjects)
When the purpose concerns SOMEONE ELSE, you use "que" + SUBJUNCTIVE:
Je lis pour que tu comprennes.
Elle parle fort afin d’être entendue.
Elle parle fort afin que les résidents l’entendent.
I’d like to read them to you, so that you can tell me if it’s too long.
This room bears his name so that his waltz never stops.

The typical mistake: "pour que" + indicative ("pour que tu dis"). Correct: "pour que tu DISES". And don’t use "pour que" with the same subject: "Je travaille pour que je réussisse" is wrong → "Je travaille pour réussir".
3. Negative purpose: de peur que, de crainte que
To say what you want to AVOID, you use "de peur que / de crainte que" + subjunctive (with an optional expletive "ne") or "de peur de / de crainte de" + infinitive:
I changed a sentence for fear she’d be embarrassed.
We need to leave early, for fear of getting stuck.

Careful: the "ne" in "de peur qu’elle NE soit gênée" is NOT a negation! The meaning is "for fear that she will be embarrassed". If you want a real negation: "de peur qu’elle ne soit PAS contente" = for fear that she will NOT be pleased.
4. De sorte que: purpose or result
J’ai mis des mouchoirs de sorte que personne ne soit pris au dépourvu.
Il a plu, de sorte que la fête a été annulée.
so that nobody is caught unprepared
it rained, so the party was cancelled
"De façon que" and "de manière que" work the same way.
de peur de, de crainte de
de peur que (ne), de crainte que (ne)
de sorte que, de façon que
Ceremony vocabulary: inaugurer une salle, couper le ruban, dévoiler une plaque (to unveil a plaque), prononcer un discours, rendre hommage à quelqu’un.
I’m reading you the text so that you can give me your opinion.
I told her gently for fear that she’d be sad.
I work in order to succeed.
Je t’explique pour que tu comprends.
J’étudie pour que je réussisse l’examen.
"I left early so as not to miss the train."
Je suis parti tôt pour ne pas rater le train.
Je suis parti tôt pour pas ne rater le train.
Je suis parti tôt pour que je ne rate pas le train.
"It rained, so we stayed at home." (result)
Il a plu, de sorte que nous soyons restés.
Il a plu, de sorte que nous sommes restés.
Il a plu, pour que nous restions.
I wrote this speech so that everyone knows.

De peur qu’Hélène ne soit gênée
Pourquoi Odile a-t-elle écrit en grosses lettres ?
Afin de pouvoir lire même en pleurant
Parce qu’elle n’a pas de lunettes
Qu’est-ce qu’Ioana a mis sur chaque chaise ?
The room bears his name so that his waltz never stops.
I want people to know who he was.

On Friday 15 September, at two in the afternoon, the Fourvière care home was like a beehive. Technicians were setting up microphones, journalists were looking for the best spot for their cameras, and Madame Lambert was running around with a list, so that nothing would be forgotten.

Ioana had arrived at noon, to check every detail. She had walked round the room ten times. The parquet gleamed. The big windows looked out onto the garden and, further away, over the whole city. On the little stage, the new piano was waiting, black and silent, under a white sheet.

Nathalie found her sitting in a corner, her eyes closed. "Are you asleep?" "No," Ioana replied. "I’m listening. I want to hear the empty room one last time, before it’s filled with music for ever." Nathalie sat down next to her, without saying anything, so as not to break the silence.

At a quarter to three, the room was full. In the front row, the residents, in their best clothes. Behind them, the families, the neighbours, the builders from the site, whom Ioana had insisted on inviting so that they could see the result of their work. At the back, thirty children from La Duchère, very well behaved, too well behaved.

The mayor arrived at three on the dot. He was a tall, smiling man who shook everyone’s hand. He gave a short speech, as promised, on the importance of culture for all generations. Then he invited Hélène and Odile to cut the ribbon together.

The two women stepped forward, arm in arm. Hélène held the scissors, Odile held the ribbon. They looked at each other for a moment. Everyone knew, without anyone saying it, that they had loved the same man, twenty years apart. The ribbon fell. The room applauded for a long time.

Then the plaque was unveiled, next to the door. A simple copper plaque, which read: "Salle Henri Bernard (1940–2023), sailor. So that the music never stops." It was the last sentence of Odile’s speech. She had suggested it to the mayor, who had accepted it at once.

Then it was Odile’s turn. She went up onto the stage with her pages written in big letters. Her voice trembled at first. But after a few sentences it grew steadier. She spoke of the sea, of Marseille, of the man who whistled a waltz every 3 May without ever saying why.

When she said "He would have loved wrong notes", one of the children at the back of the room burst out laughing, then fell silent, red with shame. Odile looked at him and smiled. "You see," she said into the microphone. "That’s exactly what he would have liked." This time the whole room laughed, and the tears flowed at the same time.

After the speeches came the moment Julien dreaded most: the orchestra’s first concert. The children had had only three rehearsals. They could play only one piece, very simple, arranged by Julien so that even the beginners could play a few notes.

Yanis was sitting behind the red-wood cello, which was almost bigger than he was. A little girl, Inès, was holding Lucien Roux’s clarinet. Her hands were shaking. In the front row, Madame Roux was leaning forward, for fear of missing the slightest note.

Julien raised his arms. There was absolute silence. Then the orchestra began. It wasn’t perfect, far from it. The violins squeaked, a flute came in too early, the drum forgot to stop. But in the middle of it all, Inès’s clarinet played its little phrase, clear and in tune, right to the end.

When the piece ended, there was a second of silence, then a storm of applause. The residents stood up, even those who no longer stood. Madame Roux was crying openly. Inès ran down from the stage and gave her back the clarinet. Madame Roux put it back in her hands. "Keep it. It’s yours."

Then Théo sat down at the new piano. The white sheet had been removed. He played Henri’s waltz, the real one, from 1962, without a score. Hélène closed her eyes. So did Odile. They were sitting side by side, and for three minutes they listened together to the music of a man each of them had lost.

The programme was over. The mayor was getting ready to leave. It was then that Radu signalled to Julien. There was one more surprise, which nobody had planned except the two of them. Radu went up onto the stage, a little nervous. "A week ago," he said, "we discovered who had given the țambal."

Everyone turned towards the back of the room. A woman of about fifty, in a cleaner’s blue overall, was standing by the door, very embarrassed. The residents all knew her: it was Mihaela, who cleaned the corridors at night, and who sometimes brought them cakes from home.

Radu had recognised her by chance, hearing her accent in the corridor. She came from a village near Botoșani, in Romanian Moldavia. The țambal had belonged to her father, a wedding musician for fifty years. After his death she had brought it to France, but she didn’t know how to play it.

"It was sleeping in a cupboard," she explained shyly, in French, with Ioana’s accent. "When I saw Monsieur Garnier’s poster, I told myself my father would have wanted a child to play it. So I left it in the morning, very quickly, before going to sleep. I didn’t want to be thanked."

Radu had called the grandmother, so that she could find someone in the village who still knew how to tune a țambal. An old cousin of Costel, the coach driver, had explained how to do it over the phone, for two hours. Radu and Lucia had spent the whole week learning a single melody.

Lucia brought the țambal onto the stage. Radu took the little sticks. Lucia took out her guitar. And together, clumsily, with lots of mistakes, they played a doina, the old sad melody of Moldavian villages, the one Mihaela’s father used to play at weddings.

Mihaela began to cry, her hand over her mouth. Hélène stood up, very slowly, and went over to her. She took her hand. And the old lady from Lyon murmured to the woman from Botoșani the three words she knew: "Mulțumesc, prietena mea." Mihaela burst into sobs in her arms.

The mayor, who had witnessed the whole scene, came over to Julien. He looked for a long time at the children, the instruments, the old ladies. "Monsieur Moreau," he said quietly, "I’m going to talk to the region. I’m not promising you anything. But I’ll do everything I can so that this project continues."

In the evening, once everyone had gone, Ioana went back into the room to turn off the lights. Hélène and Odile were still there, sitting in the front row, in the half-light. They weren’t talking. They were looking at the piano, with the lit-up city behind the big windows.

"Would you like me to leave you alone?" Ioana asked softly. Odile shook her head. "No, my dear. Stay. Sit with us." Ioana sat down between them. Hélène took one of her hands, Odile the other. They stayed like that for a long time, all three of them, in the room that bore Henri’s name.

Then Hélène stood up. She went up onto the little stage, very slowly, leaning on her cane. She sat down at the piano. She hadn’t touched a piano in fifty years. She placed a single finger on a key, the first note of the waltz, and let it ring through the empty room until it faded away.

"There," she said. "Now he’s arrived." Nobody asked what she meant. There was no need. Ioana turned off the lights one by one, leaving the last one on above the piano, so that the room wouldn’t be completely dark on its first night.

Reading text: The town hall’s invitation
The town hall has sent an official invitation to the inauguration. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
The Mayor of Lyon is pleased to invite you to the inauguration of the Salle Henri Bernard, on Friday 15 September at 3 p.m., at the Fourvière care home.
This music room was designed by Atelier Rhône so that the residents can listen to concerts without leaving their home. It will also welcome children from the neighbouring schools.
It bears the name of Henri Bernard, a sailor from Lyon, in order to pay tribute to all those who kept a piece of music in their hearts without ever being able to play it.
The programme: cutting of the ribbon, unveiling of the plaque, speeches, then the first concert, given by the pupils of the "Musique en partage" project.
We ask you to arrive before 2.45 p.m., so that the ceremony can start on time. As places are limited, please confirm your attendance.
So that the residents do not get tired, the ceremony will last no more than an hour. Refreshments will be served in the garden, under the lime tree.
